source.title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions

accepted.question_text: In the setting of integer trigonometry for triangles with integer vertices, does there exist an integer analogue of the cosine rule, comparable to the integer sine rule that is already known to hold?

evidence.quote: The integer sine rule for integer triangles holds in integer settings, while the integer cosine rule is unknown.
Problem 1. Find an integer cosine rule for integer triangles in integer trigonometry.

accepted.question_text: Classify all n-tuples of lattice length-sign sequences of the angles that can occur for integer n-gons, where the lattice length-sign sequence is the complete invariant of an integer angle in the paper’s integer-geometry setting.

evidence.quote: LLS-sequence is the complete invariant of integer angles in integer geometry.
Problem 2. (IKEA problem.) Classify all n-tuples of LLS-sequences for the angles that form integer n-gons.

accepted.question_text: Find an adequate complete invariant for polyhedra that occur as faces of sails arising in geometric multidimensional continued fractions.

evidence.quote: The following two question form the core of combinatorial and statistical problems for different sails.
• Find an adequate complete invariant of polyhedra that appear as faces at sails.

accepted.question_text: Find an adequate complete invariant of cones, up to integer congruence, in the setting of geometric multidimensional continued fractions.

evidence.quote: The following two question form the core of combinatorial and statistical problems for different sails.
• Find an adequate complete invariant of cones up to integer congruences.

accepted.question_text: Determine the face distribution of sails, that is, develop and study a generalized Gauss-Kuzmin distribution for faces in geometric multidimensional continued fractions.

evidence.quote: The following two question form the core of combinatorial and statistical problems for different sails.
• Study the face distribution of sails (generalized Gauss-Kuzmin distribution).

accepted.question_text: Classify all combinatorially possible types of faces that can occur in sails, especially for Klein polyhedra arising from geometric multidimensional continued fractions.

evidence.quote: 3.2. Faces of sails. The central question of this subsection is as follows.
Problem 3. Classify all combinatorial possible types of faces.

accepted.question_text: For each dimension n, classify all empty n-dimensional simplices up to lattice congruence, where an empty polyhedron is one whose intersection with Z^n consists exactly of its vertices.

evidence.quote: A polyhedron P is said to be empty if its intersection with Z n is precisely the set of vertices of P.
Problem 4. Classify all empty simplices of dimension n up to lattice congruence.

accepted.question_text: For given integers n and m, determine which n-gons can be realized as faces of an m-dimensional continued fraction.

evidence.quote: Problem 5. Which n-gons are realizable as faces of an m-dimensional continued fraction?

accepted.question_text: Given k runners with distinct constant speeds starting from the same point on a circular track of circumference 1, is it true that for every chosen runner there exists a time when that runner is at arc distance at least 1/k from every other runner?

evidence.quote: Problem 6. ( Lonely Runner conjecture.) Assume that k runners start a competition at the a common point of the circular track with circumference 1. Let them all have distinct constant speeds. Then for any given runner, there is a time at which that runner is lonely, i.e., at arc distance at least 1/k away from every other runners.

accepted.question_text: Describe all finite two-dimensional sails, together with the corresponding continued fractions, for the classes of multidimensional continued fractions considered in the paper.

evidence.quote: Problem 7. Describe all finite two-dimensional sails (and the corresponding continued fractions).

accepted.question_text: For polytopes of a fixed combinatorial type, describe the collections of sails of the cones associated with those polytopes; this is the multidimensional analogue of the IKEA problem discussed in the paper.

evidence.quote: The following problem is on finite continued fractions contained in the different angles of a tetrahedron.
Problem 8. (Multidimensional IKEA problem.) Describe the collections of the sails of the cones for all polytopes of a given combinatorial type.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an algorithm that decides whether a prescribed type of fundamental domain can be realized by a periodic multidimensional continued fraction?

evidence.quote: Most of further questions are related to the algebraically periodic multidimensional sails and their fundamental domains (case [A]).
Problem 9. (V. Arnold.) Does there exist an algorithm to decide whether a given type of fundamental domain is realizable by a periodic continued fraction?

accepted.question_text: If two Klein sails are integer noncongruent, must their torus decompositions be distinct? Here a torus decomposition is the collection of integer congruence types of polyhedra in a fundamental domain, together with their integer distances to the cone vertex.

evidence.quote: A torus decomposition corresponding to a periodic sail in the sense of Klein is the collections of integer congruence types of polyhedra in any fundamental domain endowed with the integer distances to the vertex of the cone.
Conjecture 10. (V. Arnold.) Torus decompositions of integer noncongruent Klein sails are distinct.

accepted.question_text: Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions.

evidence.quote: Problem 11. (V. Arnold.) Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions.

accepted.question_text: Classify the continued fractions that correspond to the same cubic extension of the field of rational numbers.

evidence.quote: In the theory of field extensions the following problem is actual.
Problem 13. (V. Arnold.) Classify continued fractions that correspond to the same cubic extension of the field of rational numbers.

accepted.question_text: For dimension n ≥ 3, prove that there exists a cone whose sail has a prescribed single non-periodic combinatorial structure.

evidence.quote: We would like to conclude this subsection with a very general problem of construction generic cones.
Problem 14. Prove the existence of a cone for a single non-periodic combinatorial structure (n ≥ 3).

accepted.question_text: For n-dimensional continued fractions, determine which faces have the highest relative frequencies.

evidence.quote: Here we would like to outline the following three questions (which are open for n ≥ 3).
Problem 15. Find frequencies on n-dimensional continued fractions with the highest relative frequencies.

accepted.question_text: For every positive integer constant C, are there only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces whose frequencies exceed C?

evidence.quote: Problem 16. For every positive integer constant C there exist only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces with frequencies exceeding C.

accepted.question_text: In dimensions n ≥ 3, is the sum of the relative frequencies of all possible faces finite?

evidence.quote: Problem 17. Is that true that sum of all relative frequencies for all possible faces is finite for higher dimensions (n ≥ 3)?

accepted.question_text: Assuming the total relative frequency of all possible faces is finite in dimensions n ≥ 3, find an appropriate generalization of the Gauss map and compare the resulting face frequencies with the frequencies coming from Möbius geometry.

evidence.quote: Problem 18. In case of positive answer to the above question find the generalization of the Gauss map and compare the corresponding frequencies of faces with the related frequencies coming from M¨obius geometry.

accepted.question_text: Find a natural generalization of the Farey tessellation in higher-dimensional hyperbolic geometry.

evidence.quote: The first question is to generalize Farey summation and its representation as a Farey tessellation.
Problem 19. Find a natural generalization of the Farey tessellation to higher-dimensional hyperbolic geometry.

accepted.question_text: Let K be a totally real cubic number field, and let y and z be elements of K with 0 < y, z < 1 such that 1, y, and z are linearly independent over Q. Must the Jacobi-Perron algorithm started from v = (1, y, z) produce an eventually periodic continued fraction?

evidence.quote: Problem 20. (Jacobi’s last theorem.) Let K be a totally real cubic number field. Consider arbitrary elements y and z of K such that 0 < y, z < 1 (here we assume that 1, y, and z are independent over Q). Is it true that the Jacobi-Perron algorithm generates an eventually periodic continued fraction with starting data v = (1, y, z).

accepted.question_text: Study the geometric properties of the Markov spectrum.

evidence.quote: The third question is related to the study of minima of decomposable forms.
Problem 21. Study geometric properties of Markov spectrum.

accepted.question_text: Generalize continued fractions so that they describe 3-bridge knots, analogously to how ordinary finite continued fractions classify rational, or two-bridge, knots.

evidence.quote: Recall that ordinary finite continued fractions provide a complete invariant to rational knots, known also as two-bridge knots.
Problem 22. Generalize continued fractions to describe 3-bridge knots.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Conjecture 12. The torus decomposition of every algebraic sail in the sense of Klein contains at least one face that is • integer congruent to a triangle; • at the unit integer distance form the vertex of the cone; • at the integer distance from the vertex of the cone greater than 1.

evidence.quote: Conjecture 12. The torus decomposition of every algebraic sail in the sense of Klein contains at least one face that is • integer congruent to a triangle; • at the unit integer distance form the vertex of the cone; • at the integer distance from the vertex of the cone greater than 1.

trace.notes: Resolved zbMATH record to arXiv:1712.01450 and mapped sections 1.3, 3.1-3.4, and 4 as the open-problem regions.
Extracted Problems 1-2 from the integer trigonometry subsection.
Extracted three unnumbered general research directions from the general directions subsection.
Extracted Problems 3-6 from the faces-of-sails subsection.
Extracted Problems 7-14 and Conjectures 10 and 12 from the combinatorial-structure subsection.
Extracted Problems 15-18 from the sail-statistics subsection.
Extracted Problems 19-22 from the final open-questions section.

Rewrote accepted items into self-contained questions by inlining minimal local definitions such as LLS-sequence, torus decomposition, and the Jacobi-Perron starting data when those details were stated in adjacent source text.
No near-duplicate questions required merging; retained one item per distinct problem or general direction.
Accepted 24 items with page-backed evidence and moved Conjecture 12 to needs_review because the scope of 'at least one face' across the three bullets is ambiguous in the source wording.
